The two produce a similar end result, one commit with the combined changes, but they work at different points and leave different history.

**`git merge --squash <branch>`** runs on the target branch (say, `main`). It stages the combined diff of `<branch>` and stops without committing. You then write a single commit yourself.
- Your feature branch is untouched.
- The new commit has only one parent, so the feature branch's commits are not in `main`'s ancestry.
- Git doesn't record that the branch was merged. If you later merge the same branch again, Git can try to re-apply changes that are already in `main`, which can cause spurious conflicts.
- Nothing is rewritten, so no force-push is needed.

**Interactive rebase with squash** (`git rebase -i main`) runs on your feature branch before you integrate it. You mark commits as `squash`/`fixup` to fold them together, and Git rewrites the branch's commits.
- The feature branch's history is replaced with the cleaned-up version.
- If you've already pushed the branch, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`, and anyone else working on it has to deal with the rewritten history.
- It's more flexible: you can also reorder, reword, split, or drop commits.
- Integration afterward is usually a fast-forward (`git merge --ff-only`), so `main` contains your cleaned commits directly and the branch ancestry is preserved. Git knows the branch was integrated.

**Rule of thumb:** use `merge --squash` (or the "Squash and merge" button on GitHub) when you want a one-step integration and don't care about the branch's internal history. Use interactive rebase when you want to tidy the branch's commits first, especially if you need to keep the history linear and avoid the re-merge problem.
